text:
Detective Howard stared at the file on his desk, the fluorescent lights of the precinct humming with a low, irritating buzz that seemed to drill into his temples. Tomorrow was his last day. He had already packed his box, said his goodbyes, and prepared to fade into the quiet anonymity of retirement. But tonight, the evidence refused to let him go.

The file contained a series of encrypted bank transfers, traced back to a shell company that funneled money into an offshore account. The signature on the authorization forms was unmistakable. It was Elias’s signature. Elias, who had pulled him out of a burning building in ’98. Elias, who had been his best man. Elias, who had promised him a drink at the bar they’d frequented for thirty years.

Howard’s hand trembled as he reached for his coffee, the cup clinking against the saucer. His duty was clear: report the fraud, initiate an internal affairs investigation, and watch his partner’s life unravel. But the cost was staggering. It wasn’t just a career; it was the foundation of Howard’s own identity. Without Elias, who was he? Just an old man with a pension and a hollow chest.

He picked up his phone, his thumb hovering over Elias’s contact name. If he called, he could warn him. He could give him a chance to explain, to run, to fix it. But that would make him an accomplice. It would taint the one clean record he had left.

The phone rang once. Twice.

"Hey, old man," Elias’s voice came through, warm and familiar, laced with the exhaustion of a long shift. "You still at the office? I was thinking we could grab that last burger before you vanish."

Howard looked at the evidence, then at the phone. The tension in his throat tightened, a physical weight pressing against his voice. He realized then that the crime wasn't just the fraud; it was the choice he had to make in the next ten seconds. To speak was to betray. To stay silent was to become a liar.

"I'm here," Howard said, his voice sounding foreign to his own ears. "But Elias... we need to talk about something else first."

He paused, the silence stretching thin and brittle. He needed to ground himself, to find a fragment of normalcy in the chaos. He thought of the simple, bright things he would miss. He thought of the way the sky looked at dusk
